Everyone believes in their own inflated ability to manage the enormous financial risks that are baked into the financial markets today.

But the people who survive monetary resets — and there have been dozens of monetary resets, in every century of every civilization — are never the cleverest traders. They are not the ones with the best read on the next Fed meeting. They are not the stock pickers or the options hedgers or the macro gurus. 

Those are the people who get wiped out. 

To survive the Fourth Turning and the coming global monetary reset, you must learn how to structure your capital in ways that are profoundly resilient. The objective when you are building a resilient strategy is not to guess the future. It is to be prepared for whatever happens next, because the one thing you can know for sure is that a bankrupt government will do everything it can to destroy you in an effort to save itself.

There is such a financial architecture. It has a name and a genealogy. It was invented almost 50 years ago by a man I knew personally, Harry Browne. I have spent the last 25 years refining this strategy at the edges, as new evidence has come in and as the monetary landscape has evolved.

Harry Browne died in 2006. That was 2 years before Lehman Brothers. It was 15 years before the COVID panic. And 20 years before the Fourth Turning had become inevitable. He was not here to see the forty-year bull market in bonds break. He was not here to see central banks resume buying gold at record pace after a generation of selling. He was not here to see Bitcoin emerge as digital gold. He was not here to see the 60/40 portfolio fail. 

But Harry’s framework — the four asset classes, the equal weights, the discipline of holding through every kind of season — is exactly the right framework for the world he did not live to see, and a testament to his genius.

I have spent 28 years applying Harry’s principle, modified by the Davis insight about insurance, sharpened by the Lindy Effect, anchored by gold and Bitcoin, and disciplined by active cash management. The result is the most resilient long-term portfolio I know how to build.

On November 3, 2009, Warren Buffett announced that Berkshire Hathaway would acquire Burlington Northern Santa Fe for $26.5 billion.
This was about six months after the market made its lows following the Global Financial Crisis, making BNSF the signature Berkshire investment of the crisis.
Berkshire had been quietly accumulating BNSF stock in the open market since August 2006, three years earlier. It already owned 22.5% of the railroad. The position could have been built out quarter by quarter, share by share, at market prices, in the same way Buffett built Berkshire’s position in Coca-Cola 20 years earlier. He chose not to. On November 3, he telephoned Matt Rose, BNSF’s CEO, and offered to buy the remaining 77.5% in a single transaction at $100 per share. And Berkshire, at that moment, locked itself into a transaction whose full arithmetic the financial press has never properly understood.
Here is the deal, in numbers.
Consideration for the 77.5% Berkshire did not already own: $26.5 billion. Of that, $15.9 billion was paid in cash. Of that cash, roughly half was drawn from Berkshire’s balance sheet, and the other half — about $8 billion — was raised through new corporate debt issued at the Berkshire parent level. The remaining $10.6 billion of the purchase price was paid in Berkshire stock.
Buffett issued 80,931 Class A shares and 20,976,621 Class B shares to buy his railroad. At the $80,000-per-share level at which Berkshire traded that day, those shares were worth $10.6 billion. At today’s price, the same shares are worth approximately $73 billion.
Later, Buffett would write about the deal: 
“In our BNSF acquisition, the selling shareholders quite properly evaluated our offer at $100 per share. The cost to us, however, was somewhat higher since 40% of the $100 was delivered in our shares, which Charlie and I believed to be worth more than their market value.”
That's the understatement of his career. 
That $73 billion — the present-day value of what Berkshire gave up in it own shares — is larger than the entire current market capitalization of Union Pacific. It is larger than the combined current market cap of CSX and Norfolk Southern.
Buffett used the best currency in capitalism to buy the worst-performing asset in its industry, and then he committed Berkshire to spending $22 billion of additional capital over the next fourteen years just to keep the asset running in place.

And this huge mistake is about to get a lot worse. 

In his 2023 letter, Buffett wrote that BNSF’s dividends to Berkshire “will regularly fall considerably short of BNSF’s reported earnings unless we regularly increase the railroad’s debt. And that we do not intend to do.”
Translated: Berkshire had been using BNSF’s balance sheet to finance a portion of its capital shortfalls each year. Now, when BNSF needs more capital than it produces, it will not be able to add any further debt. For fourteen years, a meaningful share of BNSF’s annual capital budget has come from the credit markets. Buffett has now drawn the line. The debt will not grow further.
That decision has a consequence that does not appear in any Berkshire annual letter. If BNSF cannot add incremental debt, and if BNSF’s capital expenditures continue to exceed depreciation by a billion dollars or more every year, then BNSF’s dividends to Berkshire have to fall. Either capex gets cut — with predictable consequences for a physical network whose core asset is already compounding at a slower rate than its depreciation — or the dividends shrink. There is no third option.
The dividends have already begun to shrink. In 2020, BNSF paid Berkshire $4.8 billion. In 2022, $5.0 billion. In 2023, it fell to $3.1 billion. In 2024, it recovered to $4.0 billion — still below 2020. The cumulative 2010-through-2020 distributions Buffett so proudly cited in the 2020 letter — “$41.8 billion in total” — averaged roughly $3.8 billion a year across that decade. The 2023 and 2024 figures are running at or below that long-run average, despite inflation, despite revenue growth, despite fourteen years of capital-expenditure investment that was supposed to compound into higher earnings power.
The capital went in. Most of it did not come back out. And more and more of it never will
